meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Melancholy Is the Pleasure of Being Sad'?
meta.ogDescription: Mencken did not say this. He quoted it, correctly attributed, in his dictionary of quotations — and got the credit anyway.

answer.label: Not H.L. Mencken — actually Victor Hugo
answer.sourceLine: Hugo wrote it in Les Travailleurs de la Mer (1866): “La mélancolie, c’est le bonheur d’être triste.” The exact English words people quote come from the authorized translation published the same year by W. Moy Thomas, where the line appears on page 159 of volume III. Mencken gets the credit only because he reprinted it in his 1942 New Dictionary of Quotations — under Hugo’s name, correctly cited.

source.heading: The source

source.excerpt: “Despair has its backward stages. From overwhelmment we rise to dejection; from dejection to affliction; from affliction to melancholy. Melancholy is a twilight state; suffering melts into it and becomes a sombre joy. Melancholy is the pleasure of being sad.”
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ concludes that “Victor Hugo should be credited with this statement which was originally constructed in French by 1866,” and reproduces the French from Les Travailleurs de la Mer: “La mélancolie, c’est le bonheur d’être triste.” QI cites the 1866 Librairie Internationale edition, volume 2, page 154 — a page we did not read ourselves.

Which English translation? QI notes only that “Mencken used a different translation” and does not name it. We found it. The scanned third volume of the authorized English translation by W. Moy Thomas (London: Sampson Low, Son, & Marston, 1866) carries the sentence verbatim on page 159: “Melancholy is the pleasure of being sad.” The full scan, title page and all ↗

Mencken’s own citation points at that same edition. QI reproduces his entry ↗ as “Melancholy is the pleasure of being sad. VICTOR HUGO: The Toilers of the Sea, III, 1866” — volume III, 1866, which is exactly the Moy Thomas edition. Mencken does not name a translator anywhere in the entry, so the identification is ours rather than his: the wording he printed is the one Moy Thomas published, and his citation points at the volume it is in.

Two other English renderings exist and neither matches the popular wording: Isabel F. Hapgood’s 1888 translation has “Melancholy is the happiness of being sad,” and James Hogarth’s 2002 version has “Melancholy is the enjoyment of being sad.” Both per Quote Investigator ↗.
source.excerptNote: The sentence is the last step of a ladder, not an aphorism on its own. Hugo is describing how the shipowner Lethierry climbs out of ruin — despair rising by degrees until it settles into something almost pleasant.

sourceLink.text: Read the 1866 authorized translation, vol. III

source.rightsNote: Clear on both counts. Hugo’s French original was published in 1866 and he died in 1885; the English wording quoted here comes from W. Moy Thomas’s authorized translation of the same year, and Thomas died in 1910. Both are far beyond the 1931 United States copyright cut-off, so this sentence is in the public domain. Note that Mencken’s 1942 dictionary is not — but you do not need it, because the 1866 translation is the earlier and better source.

author.bio: Victor Hugo was a French Romantic author, poet, playwright and politician, best known for The Hunchback of Notre-Dame (1831) and Les Misérables (1862). Les Travailleurs de la Mer followed in 1866 and is dedicated to Guernsey, where Hugo spent fifteen years in exile; the story turns on a Guernsey shipowner, Mess Lethierry, whose vessel is wrecked on a reef. The ladder of despair this quotation completes is very much his register — an abstraction stated as flatly as a fact, dropped into the middle of a story about a wrecked steamship.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This is a misattribution with an innocent culprit. Mencken compiled a dictionary of other people’s quotations, attributed this one properly, and then had it stick to him anyway.

items.why: Mencken printed the line in A New Dictionary of Quotations on Historical Principles (1942), in its Melancholy section on page 777, under the heading “VICTOR HUGO: The Toilers of the Sea, III, 1866.” He was the editor of the book it appears in, not the author of the sentence. Quote Investigator ↗
“La mélancolie, c’est le bonheur d’être triste” — Les Travailleurs de la Mer, 1866. QI’s conclusion ↗ is unambiguous: Hugo should be credited.

The specific English words that circulate are his, from the authorized translation of 1866 — not Hapgood’s 1888 “happiness” nor Hogarth’s 2002 “enjoyment.” Thomas (1828–1910) ↗ was an English journalist and literary editor, and is almost never named alongside the quotation. His translation, vol. III, p. 159 ↗

misattribution.truthLine: Hugo wrote it; Moy Thomas gave it these English words; Mencken merely filed it correctly. Quote Investigator’s full account ↗

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Read in place, the line is not a pretty thought about sadness — it is the top of a staircase. Hugo has his ruined shipowner Mess Lethierry climbing out of catastrophe by stages: overwhelmment, dejection, affliction, and finally melancholy, which Hugo calls “a twilight state.” The sentence about pleasure is the arrival, and it is meant to sound like relief rather than indulgence.
Hugo then takes it straight back: “These elegiac moods were not made for Lethierry.” The most-quoted sentence in the passage describes a consolation the character is specifically denied.
detailsBody: How the credit moved to Mencken is easy to reconstruct, and it is a pattern worth recognising. A big, authoritative reference book is the place a great many quotations are looked up; strip one line out of it and the compiler’s name is the name still attached to the page. Mencken’s New Dictionary of Quotations was a monument of exactly that kind, and the transfer happens to him more than once.

The translator’s disappearance is the quieter loss. “Pleasure,” “happiness” and “enjoyment” are three different readings of Hugo’s bonheur, and it is the first — W. Moy Thomas’s, printed in the novel’s own year of publication — that English readers ended up memorising. He is credited nowhere in the popular quotation.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes "Victor Hugo should be credited with this statement which was originally constructed in French by 1866", quotes the French "La mélancolie, c’est le bonheur d’être triste" from Les Travailleurs de la Mer (1866), reproduces Mencken’s 1942 A New Dictionary of Quotations entry (p. 777) reading "Melancholy is the pleasure of being sad. VICTOR HUGO: The Toilers of the Sea, III, 1866", notes Mencken used a different translation without naming it, and gives Hapgood’s 1888 "happiness of being sad" and Hogarth’s 2002 "enjoyment of being sad".

This scan’s title page reads "TOILERS OF THE SEA, By VICTOR HUGO … AUTHORIZED ENGLISH TRANSLATION, BY W. MOY THOMAS. IN THREE VOLUMES. Vol. III. LONDON: SAMPSON LOW, SON, & MARSTON … 1866." On page 159, in the Third Part, Book I ("Night and the Moon"), chapter I ("The Harbour Clock"), it reads: "Despair has its backward stages. From overwhelmment we rise to dejection; from dejection to affliction; from affliction to melancholy. Melancholy is a twilight state; suffering melts into it and becomes a sombre joy. Melancholy is the pleasure of being sad. These elegiac moods were not made for Lethierry." The phrase occurs exactly once in the volume.

Victor-Marie Hugo (26 February 1802 – 22 May 1885) was a French Romantic author, poet, essayist, playwright and politician, best known for The Hunchback of Notre-Dame (1831) and Les Misérables (1862).
Henry Louis Mencken (September 12, 1880 – January 29, 1956) was an American journalist, essayist, satirist, cultural critic and scholar of American English.
William Moy Thomas (1828–1910) was an English journalist, literary editor and novelist.
Wikipedia has an article on Hugo’s 1866 novel Toilers of the Sea.

Toilers of the Sea (Les Travailleurs de la mer) is a novel by Victor Hugo published in 1866, dedicated to the island of Guernsey where Hugo spent 15 years in exile; the story concerns a Guernseyman named Gilliatt and Deruchette, niece of a local shipowner, Mess Lethierry, whose ship is wrecked on the double Douvres reef.
